title: We feel more like roommates than partners
summary: Feel more like roommates than partners? Why the drift happens, what you both stopped saying, and small ways to start turning back toward each other.
body_markdown:
You split the bills fairly. You know each other's coffee order and work schedule. Nobody slams doors. And then some evening, sitting at opposite ends of the couch, it hits you: we live together, we get along, and I'm not sure we're actually together anymore.


There's a name going around for where this can end up. On a September 15, 2026 episode of KQED's Forum, psychologist Thema Bryant and Northwestern researcher Eli Finkel talked through what's being called a "quiet divorce": two people who stay married and physically present while one or both of them has gone emotionally absent. If that phrase landed a little close, you're not the only one living some version of it. But the name matters less than what it points to. A quiet divorce doesn't happen all at once. It's what the roommate phase becomes when nobody says anything.


Which means if you're reading this, you're probably earlier than that. You noticed. That's the step most couples skip.


## Which kind of roommates are you?


People use the word for a few different things, and it helps to know which one you've got.


- **Parallel lives.** You each have your evening routine, your shows, your phone, your side of the bed. You rarely fight because you're rarely in the same moment.
- **Friendly but flat.** You're kind to each other. You'd call yourselves friends. But nothing gets shared that you wouldn't tell a coworker: no worries, no half-formed ideas, no "I've been feeling off lately."
- **Touch went quiet.** Not only sex. The hand on the back walking past, the kiss that isn't a goodbye. Physical closeness is often the first thing to fade and the last thing anyone mentions.
- **You've stopped expecting anything.** This is the one to pay attention to. Not anger, not hurt. Just a shrug where wanting used to be.


The first three are common and very reversible. The fourth is where drift starts to harden, because once neither of you is reaching, there's nothing left for the other person to respond to.


## Busy is a different problem


If your whole relationship has been swallowed by school runs and shared calendars, that's real, but it's a slightly different thing: the version where[the couple turns into a logistics team](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/weve-become-a-logistics-team-not-a-couple) . Busy couples usually still light up when they finally get an hour alone. Roommates are what's left when the hour shows up and you don't know what to do with it. The time is there. The turning toward each other isn't.


That matters because the fix for busy is protecting time. The fix for roommates is harder, and honestly more interesting: getting back the habit of telling each other things.


## It usually starts with conversations you skipped


When people bring this to Maia, they almost never open with "we've drifted apart." They open with something oddly small. They told a friend about a big conversation at work before they told their partner, and only noticed three days later. They catch themselves rehearsing what they'll say to their partner, the way you'd prep for a meeting. Or they describe a fight they almost had about the dishwasher, and then didn't, because it didn't seem worth it.


That last one shows up in a lot of forms. The roommate phase is mostly built out of skipped conversations, not dramatic ones. Each skip is reasonable on its own. You're tired, it's minor, they seem stressed. But every one is a moment where you decided the relationship could hold one more silence. After a year or two, it can hold a lot of silence, and not much else.


## A better question than "are we quietly divorced?"


That question isn't useful. It pushes you toward a verdict you probably aren't ready to make, and it makes the whole thing feel bigger and more fixed than it is.


Try this one instead: **what did we stop saying to each other, and when?**


Most people can find it if they look. The stretch after a baby. The year one of you was job hunting and the other learned not to ask. The money argument that never really ended, it just stopped being said out loud. Find the rough starting point and you usually find the thing still sitting in the room, which tells you what the first real conversation needs to be about. If the honest answer is "we stopped bringing up anything hard," that has its own shape, and[avoiding hard conversations and letting things build up](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/we-avoid-hard-conversations) is often exactly what roommate-ness is made of.


## Small ways back in


- **Say one unedited thing a day.** Not a status report. Something you'd normally keep to yourself: a worry, a strange thought, a thing that made you laugh. It feels exposing the first few times. That's how you know it's doing something.
- **Name it once, without building a case.** "I miss us. I don't think either of us did anything wrong. I just feel like we've been living next to each other." No list of evidence. Evidence turns it into a trial.
- **Bring touch back below the level of sex.** A hand on a shoulder. Sitting on the same cushion. Low stakes on purpose, so neither of you has to wonder where it's heading.
- **Get curious about the person you stopped checking on.** People keep changing. The partner you filed away five years ago isn't quite the one making coffee now.[Being present with your partner](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/mindfulness-hacks-for-couples-4-secrets-to-being-present) is mostly paying attention like they're still new information.


What tends to backfire is the big reset. A weekend away with enormous pressure on it, or a "we need to talk about us" sit-down both of you dread. Those can work, but they often buy one nice evening and then the same couch on Monday. Here, small and daily beats big and rare.


## When it's more than drift


Sometimes you try all of this and get nothing back. You reach and they don't reach back, or they're pleasant about it and nothing changes. That can mean your partner checked out a while ago, or that something is going on for them they haven't said yet. Either way, ask directly. Reaching harder won't answer it.


And if you read this far and thought, honestly, I'm not sure I want to find the way back, that's a different question and a fair one. It deserves its own room, not a tip list.[Deciding whether to break up or keep trying](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/should-i-break-up-or-keep-trying) is a real decision, and so is noticing[that another year has gone by like this](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/should-this-be-the-year-i-leave) . Either answer can be the right one. Sliding into one without looking is the thing to avoid.


If you want to figure out where the quiet started in your relationship, or find a way to say "I miss us" that won't land like an accusation, Maia can help you think it through, on your own first or together with your partner. The first sentence is usually the hardest part, and it's easier to find with someone neutral in the room.
